claim: Vitamin D deficiency has been associated with the rise in chronic inflammatory diseases, including asthma.
source: Vitamin D possesses immunomodulatory functions and vitamin D deficiency has been associated with the rise in chronic inflammatory diseases, including asthma (Litonjua and Weiss, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Litonjua and Weiss, 2007

claim: Vitamin D regulates the Chr17q12-21.1 chromosomal locus.
source: Here, we provide evidence for vitamin D regulation of two human chromosomal loci, Chr17q12-21.1 and Chr17q21.2, reliably associated with autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases.
evidence: Demonstrated through bioinformatic analysis and experimental data in the manuscript

claim: Vitamin D regulates the Chr17q21.2 chromosomal locus.
source: Here, we provide evidence for vitamin D regulation of two human chromosomal loci, Chr17q12-21.1 and Chr17q21.2, reliably associated with autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases.
evidence: Demonstrated through bioinformatic analysis and experimental data in the manuscript

claim: Chr17q12-21.1 and Chr17q21.2 are reliably associated with autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases.
source: Here, we provide evidence for vitamin D regulation of two human chromosomal loci, Chr17q12-21.1 and Chr17q21.2, reliably associated with autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases.
evidence: Based on GWAS catalog data and established scientific knowledge

claim: Vitamin D receptor (Vdr) expression is increased in mouse lung CD4+ Th2 cells.
source: We demonstrate increased vitamin D receptor (Vdr) expression in mouse lung CD4+ Th2 cells, differential expression of Chr17q12-21.1 and Chr17q21.2 genes in Th2 cells based on vitamin D status and identify the IL-2/Stat5 pathway as a target of vitamin D signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry and Western blot analysis in the manuscript

claim: Chr17q12-21.1 and Chr17q21.2 genes are differentially expressed in Th2 cells based on vitamin D status.
source: We demonstrate increased vitamin D receptor (Vdr) expression in mouse lung CD4+ Th2 cells, differential expression of Chr17q12-21.1 and Chr17q21.2 genes in Th2 cells based on vitamin D status and identify the IL-2/Stat5 pathway as a target of vitamin D signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis comparing WT and vitamin D-deficient Th2 cultures

claim: The IL-2/Stat5 pathway is a target of vitamin D signaling.
source: We demonstrate increased vitamin D receptor (Vdr) expression in mouse lung CD4+ Th2 cells, differential expression of Chr17q12-21.1 and Chr17q21.2 genes in Th2 cells based on vitamin D status and identify the IL-2/Stat5 pathway as a target of vitamin D signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq, pathway enrichment analysis, and experimental validation

claim: Vitamin D deficiency caused severe lung inflammation after allergen challenge in mice.
source: Vitamin D deficiency caused severe lung inflammation after allergen challenge in mice that was prevented by long-term prenatal vitamin D supplementation.
evidence: Demonstrated by histology, BAL cell counts, and flow cytometry in HDM-challenged mice

claim: Long-term prenatal vitamin D supplementation prevented severe lung inflammation after allergen challenge in mice.
source: Vitamin D deficiency caused severe lung inflammation after allergen challenge in mice that was prevented by long-term prenatal vitamin D supplementation.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing mice supplemented with different vitamin D doses over two generations

claim: Vitamin D induces the expression of the Ikzf3-encoded protein Aiolos.
source: Mechanistically, vitamin D induced the expression of the Ikzf3-encoded protein Aiolos to suppress IL-2 signaling and ameliorate cytokine production in Th2 cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry showing increased Aiolos expression after calcitriol stimulation

claim: Aiolos suppresses IL-2 signaling in Th2 cells.
source: Mechanistically, vitamin D induced the expression of the Ikzf3-encoded protein Aiolos to suppress IL-2 signaling and ameliorate cytokine production in Th2 cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments with Ikzf3−/− mice showing reduced vitamin D-mediated suppression of IL-2

claim: Aiolos ameliorates cytokine production in Th2 cells.
source: Mechanistically, vitamin D induced the expression of the Ikzf3-encoded protein Aiolos to suppress IL-2 signaling and ameliorate cytokine production in Th2 cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by reduced IL-13 production in calcitriol-stimulated Th2 cells

claim: The vitamin D receptor was genetically associated with asthma in 2004.
source: The vitamin D receptor was genetically associated with asthma in 2004 (Raby et al., 2004) and high intake of vitamin D by pregnant women is associated with about a 50% reduction in asthma risk in the mother's offspring (Camargo et al., 2007; Devereux et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raby et al., 2004

claim: High intake of vitamin D by pregnant women is associated with about a 50% reduction in asthma risk in the mother's offspring.
source: The vitamin D receptor was genetically associated with asthma in 2004 (Raby et al., 2004) and high intake of vitamin D by pregnant women is associated with about a 50% reduction in asthma risk in the mother's offspring (Camargo et al., 2007; Devereux et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Camargo et al., 2007 and Devereux et al., 2007

claim: Progressive decreases in vitamin D intake from 1946 onward could be contributing to the epidemic of allergic and autoimmune diseases.
source: Together, these findings led to a comprehensive theory about how vitamin D deficiency could influence asthma occurrence through its effects on lung and immune system development and that progressive decreases in vitamin D intake from 1946 onward could be contributing to the epidemic of allergic and autoimmune diseases (Litonjua and Weiss, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Litonjua and Weiss, 2007

claim: Vitamin D deficiency is the most common vitamin deficiency in the world today.
source: Vitamin D deficiency is the most common vitamin deficiency in the world today and is particularly prevalent in pregnant women where the fetal lung and immune system are developing in utero (van der Pligt et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2018; Cashman, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to van der Pligt et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2018; Cashman, 2020

claim: Vitamin D deficiency is particularly prevalent in pregnant women.
source: Vitamin D deficiency is the most common vitamin deficiency in the world today and is particularly prevalent in pregnant women where the fetal lung and immune system are developing in utero (van der Pligt et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2018; Cashman, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to van der Pligt et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2018; Cashman, 2020

claim: The SNP rs12936231 is located in ZPBP2, the gene adjacent to ORMDL3.
source: To link the results of the VDAART trial directly to the chr17q12 locus, our group then genotyped the single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) rs12936231, located in ZPBP2, the gene adjacent to ORMDL3, and stratified the VDAART trial results by maternal genotype at this locus.
evidence: Based on genomic location data

claim: The vitamin D effect in the VDAART trial was significantly influenced by genotype at rs12936231.
source: This study found that the vitamin D effect in the trial was significantly influenced by genotype, with the GG genotype exhibiting a protective effect on asthma risk in the child and the CC or GC genotype not being responsive to vitamin D; additionally, this result was related to sphingolipid production with the children protected from asthma having higher sphingolipid production (Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelly et al., 2019

claim: The GG genotype at rs12936231 exhibits a protective effect on asthma risk in children.
source: This study found that the vitamin D effect in the trial was significantly influenced by genotype, with the GG genotype exhibiting a protective effect on asthma risk in the child and the CC or GC genotype not being responsive to vitamin D; additionally, this result was related to sphingolipid production with the children protected from asthma having higher sphingolipid production (Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelly et al., 2019

claim: The CC or GC genotype at rs12936231 is not responsive to vitamin D.
source: This study found that the vitamin D effect in the trial was significantly influenced by genotype, with the GG genotype exhibiting a protective effect on asthma risk in the child and the CC or GC genotype not being responsive to vitamin D; additionally, this result was related to sphingolipid production with the children protected from asthma having higher sphingolipid production (Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelly et al., 2019

claim: Children protected from asthma have higher sphingolipid production.
source: This study found that the vitamin D effect in the trial was significantly influenced by genotype, with the GG genotype exhibiting a protective effect on asthma risk in the child and the CC or GC genotype not being responsive to vitamin D; additionally, this result was related to sphingolipid production with the children protected from asthma having higher sphingolipid production (Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelly et al., 2019

claim: Rs12936231 and rs4065275 alter the chromatin state of a regulatory domain in the chr17q12-21.1 locus.
source: This SNP (rs12936231) is one of two SNPs (the other being rs4065275) that alter the chromatin state of a regulatory domain, specifically two CTCF-binding sites, in the chr17q12-21.1 locus that are correlated with the expression of ORMDL3 (Schmiedel et al., 2016; Verlaan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schmiedel et al., 2016 and Verlaan et al., 2009

claim: Rs12936231 and rs4065275 affect two CTCF-binding sites in the chr17q12-21.1 locus.
source: This SNP (rs12936231) is one of two SNPs (the other being rs4065275) that alter the chromatin state of a regulatory domain, specifically two CTCF-binding sites, in the chr17q12-21.1 locus that are correlated with the expression of ORMDL3 (Schmiedel et al., 2016; Verlaan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schmiedel et al., 2016 and Verlaan et al., 2009

claim: Rs12936231 and rs4065275 are correlated with the expression of ORMDL3.
source: This SNP (rs12936231) is one of two SNPs (the other being rs4065275) that alter the chromatin state of a regulatory domain, specifically two CTCF-binding sites, in the chr17q12-21.1 locus that are correlated with the expression of ORMDL3 (Schmiedel et al., 2016; Verlaan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schmiedel et al., 2016 and Verlaan et al., 2009

claim: The ORMDL3 promoter interacts with a long-range enhancer in IKZF3.
source: 4C-seq assays previously demonstrated that the ORMDL3 promoter interacts with a long-range enhancer in IKZF3 that promotes (or represses) transcription of ORMDL3 in cells expressing both genes and the binding of CTCF per the G allele of rs12936231 in ZPBP2 blocks this interaction, resulting in reduced transcription of ORMDL3 on haplotypes with the rs12936231-G allele (Schmiedel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmiedel et al., 2016

claim: The binding of CTCF per the G allele of rs12936231 in ZPBP2 blocks the interaction between the ORMDL3 promoter and the IKZF3 enhancer.
source: 4C-seq assays previously demonstrated that the ORMDL3 promoter interacts with a long-range enhancer in IKZF3 that promotes (or represses) transcription of ORMDL3 in cells expressing both genes and the binding of CTCF per the G allele of rs12936231 in ZPBP2 blocks this interaction, resulting in reduced transcription of ORMDL3 on haplotypes with the rs12936231-G allele (Schmiedel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmiedel et al., 2016

claim: Haplotypes with the rs12936231-G allele have reduced transcription of ORMDL3.
source: 4C-seq assays previously demonstrated that the ORMDL3 promoter interacts with a long-range enhancer in IKZF3 that promotes (or represses) transcription of ORMDL3 in cells expressing both genes and the binding of CTCF per the G allele of rs12936231 in ZPBP2 blocks this interaction, resulting in reduced transcription of ORMDL3 on haplotypes with the rs12936231-G allele (Schmiedel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmiedel et al., 2016

claim: Mice expressing the ORMDL3 transgene exhibit spontaneous increases in airway hyper responsiveness (AHR).
source: Mouse models have contributed to our understanding of ORMDL3 function as mice expressing the ORMDL3 transgene exhibit spontaneous increases in airway hyper responsiveness (AHR), the essential feature of asthma.
evidence: Based on mouse model studies

claim: The increase in AHR in ORMDL3 transgenic mice was associated with airway remodeling and peri bronchial fibrosis without airway inflammation.
source: This increase in AHR was associated with airway remodeling and peri bronchial fibrosis without airway inflammation (Miller et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller et al., 2014

claim: Increased expression of ORMDL3 inhibits the enzyme serine palmityl-transferase.
source: Most importantly, increased expression of ORMDL3 inhibits the enzyme serine palmityl-transferase, the rate limiting step in the production of sphingolipids, and ORMDL3 transgenic mice have reduced levels of sphingolipids (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2019

claim: Serine palmityl-transferase is the rate limiting step in the production of sphingolipids.
source: Most importantly, increased expression of ORMDL3 inhibits the enzyme serine palmityl-transferase, the rate limiting step in the production of sphingolipids, and ORMDL3 transgenic mice have reduced levels of sphingolipids (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2019 and established biochemical knowledge

claim: ORMDL3 transgenic mice have reduced levels of sphingolipids.
source: Most importantly, increased expression of ORMDL3 inhibits the enzyme serine palmityl-transferase, the rate limiting step in the production of sphingolipids, and ORMDL3 transgenic mice have reduced levels of sphingolipids (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2019

claim: Chr17q12-21.1 had the highest number of associations related to Th2 diseases.
source: Chr17q12-21.1 had the highest number of associations related to Th2 diseases (Figure 1A) and 17q21.2 had the highest number of associations related to Th1 diseases (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of GWAS catalog data shown in Figure 1A

claim: 17q21.2 had the highest number of associations related to Th1 diseases.
source: Chr17q12-21.1 had the highest number of associations related to Th2 diseases (Figure 1A) and 17q21.2 had the highest number of associations related to Th1 diseases (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of GWAS catalog data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Seven VDR-binding sites on Chr17 are in the 17q12-21.1 locus.
source: Out of the 169 VDR-binding sites on Chr17, seven were in the 17q12-21.1 locus, concentrated in two bands on or near IKZF3 and ZPBP2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: VDR-binding sites in the 17q12-21.1 locus are concentrated in two bands on or near IKZF3 and ZPBP2.
source: Out of the 169 VDR-binding sites on Chr17, seven were in the 17q12-21.1 locus, concentrated in two bands on or near IKZF3 and ZPBP2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: VDR-binding sites overlap with RXRA-binding sites in the 17q12-21.1 locus.
source: These VDR-binding sites also overlapped with RXRA-binding sites (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: Four cis-eQTLs control IKZF3 expression in whole blood and EBV-transformed lymphocytes.
source: We found that four cis-eQTLs control IKZF3 expression in whole blood and EBV-transformed lymphocytes: rs2941522 and rs12946510 in the enhancer region targeting ORMDL3 and IKZF3, and rs1453559 and rs35564481 in the enhancer region targeting ORMDL3, GSDMA, and GSDMB (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by eQTL analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: Rs1453559 and rs2941522 have previous GWAS associations with both asthma and autoimmune diseases.
source: Rs1453559 and rs2941522 have previous Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) associations with both asthma and autoimmune diseases (Syreeni et al., 2021; Shrine et al., 2019; Marinho et al., 2012), rs12946510 has previous GWAS associations with autoimmune diseases (Hitomi et al., 2017; Keshari et al., 2016), and rs35564481 has no known GWAS associations.
evidence: Supported by citations to Syreeni et al., 2021; Shrine et al., 2019; Marinho et al., 2012

claim: Rs12946510 has previous GWAS associations with autoimmune diseases.
source: Rs1453559 and rs2941522 have previous Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) associations with both asthma and autoimmune diseases (Syreeni et al., 2021; Shrine et al., 2019; Marinho et al., 2012), rs12946510 has previous GWAS associations with autoimmune diseases (Hitomi et al., 2017; Keshari et al., 2016), and rs35564481 has no known GWAS associations.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hitomi et al., 2017; Keshari et al., 2016

claim: Rs35564481 has no known GWAS associations.
source: Rs1453559 and rs2941522 have previous Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) associations with both asthma and autoimmune diseases (Syreeni et al., 2021; Shrine et al., 2019; Marinho et al., 2012), rs12946510 has previous GWAS associations with autoimmune diseases (Hitomi et al., 2017; Keshari et al., 2016), and rs35564481 has no known GWAS associations.
evidence: Based on GWAS catalog search

claim: The only VDR-binding site in the 17q21.2 locus resides near the gene PSMC3IP in an enhancer site targeting STAT5A.
source: For the 17q21.2 locus, the only VDR-binding site resides near the gene PSMC3IP in an enhancer site targeting STAT5A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: PSMC3IP expression is controlled by three eQTLs overlapping with the VDR-binding site near PSMC3IP.
source: PSMC3IP expression is controlled by three eQTLs overlapping with this VDR-binding site (rs4793244, rs62078362, and rs111708606), none of which have any known disease associations.
evidence: Demonstrated by eQTL analysis

claim: The interaction between vitamin D and IKZF3 expression was statistically significant in predicting asthma risk at age 3 years.
source: After adjusting for relevant covariates (see Methods), the baseline expression term of IKZF3 was not found to be significantly associated with asthma risk, while the interaction between vitamin D and IKZF3 was statistically significant (p-val. <0.05), suggesting that the association of IKZF3 expression with asthma risk was mediated by vitamin D levels in the CB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by logistic regression analysis of VDAART cord blood data

claim: The association of IKZF3 expression with asthma risk is mediated by vitamin D levels in cord blood.
source: After adjusting for relevant covariates (see Methods), the baseline expression term of IKZF3 was not found to be significantly associated with asthma risk, while the interaction between vitamin D and IKZF3 was statistically significant (p-val. <0.05), suggesting that the association of IKZF3 expression with asthma risk was mediated by vitamin D levels in the CB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Inferred from statistical analysis showing significant interaction term

claim: Vdr expression was significantly induced in HDM sensitized and challenged mice.
source: Vdr expression was significantly induced in HDM sensitized and challenged mice and almost absent in leukocytes isolated from control (vehicle) lungs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: Vdr expression was almost absent in leukocytes isolated from control (vehicle) lungs.
source: Vdr expression was significantly induced in HDM sensitized and challenged mice and almost absent in leukocytes isolated from control (vehicle) lungs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: Vdr expression was high in CD4+ T cells within the CD45+ population.
source: Within the CD45+ population, Vdr expression was high in CD4+ T cells (p = 0.0357), while only very few CD8+ T cells and CD19+ B cells expressed Vdr (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B HDM).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: Only very few CD8+ T cells and CD19+ B cells expressed Vdr.
source: Within the CD45+ population, Vdr expression was high in CD4+ T cells (p = 0.0357), while only very few CD8+ T cells and CD19+ B cells expressed Vdr (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B HDM).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Highest Vdr expression within CD4+ T cells was detected in Gata3+ Th2 cells.
source: Within the CD4+ T cell population, highest Vdr expression was detected in Gata3+ Th2 cells (p = 0.002 vs Tbet+ and p < 0.0001 vs Foxp3+ T cells).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis

claim: Vdr expression was very low in Tbet+ Th1 and CD4+Foxp3+ Treg cells.
source: Vdr expression was very low in Tbet+ Th1 and CD4+Foxp3+ Treg cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C HDM).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: Vdr expression appeared as early as day 1 of Th2 culture conditions.
source: Vdr expression appeared as early as day 1 of Th2 culture conditions and gradually increased during the polarization process (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: Vdr expression gradually increased during the Th2 polarization process.
source: Vdr expression appeared as early as day 1 of Th2 culture conditions and gradually increased during the polarization process (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: In the absence of vitamin D, Vdr expression localized to the cytoplasm of Th2 cells.
source: In the absence of the Vdr ligand vitamin D, Vdr expression localized to the cytoplasm of Th2 cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy

claim: Addition of calcitriol led to a strong translocation of Vdr into the nucleus of Th2 cells.
source: Addition of the Vdr ligand calcitriol led to a strong translocation of Vdr into the nucleus, suggesting functionality of the expressed receptor in the presence of its ligand (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 3 and 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: Vitamin D deficiency differentially regulated the expression levels of several Chr17q12-21.1-encoded genes.
source: Vitamin D deficiency differentially regulated the expression levels of several Chr17q12-21.1-encoded genes, with lower expression of Ikzf3, Ormdl3, and Gsdma (all p = 0.0286) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: Vitamin D deficiency resulted in lower expression of Ikzf3, Ormdl3, and Gsdma in Th2 cells.
source: Vitamin D deficiency differentially regulated the expression levels of several Chr17q12-21.1-encoded genes, with lower expression of Ikzf3, Ormdl3, and Gsdma (all p = 0.0286) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: Calcitriol stimulation induced the expression of Ikzf3, Ormdl3, and Gsdma in Th2 cells.
source: Conversely, stimulation with calcitriol induced the expression of the same genes (all p = 0.043) (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2F

claim: Expression of Stat3, Stat5a, and Stat5b was not affected by vitamin D deficiency in Th2 cells.
source: Expression of the Chr17q21.2 genes Stat3, Stat5a, and Stat5b was not affected by vitamin D deficiency (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: Calcitriol stimulation strongly suppressed Stat5a and Stat5b gene expression in Th2 cells.
source: However, after calcitriol stimulation Stat5a (p = 0.0082) and Stat5b (p = 0.003) genes were strongly suppressed and Stat3 (p = 0.0048) expression was increased in Th2 cells. (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: Calcitriol stimulation increased Stat3 expression in Th2 cells.
source: However, after calcitriol stimulation Stat5a (p = 0.0082) and Stat5b (p = 0.003) genes were strongly suppressed and Stat3 (p = 0.0048) expression was increased in Th2 cells. (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: HDM sensitization of vitamin D-deficient mice led to a stronger reaction to the allergen resulting in more prominent peri-bronchial and perivascular leukocytic infiltrates.
source: HDM sensitization of vitamin D-deficient mice led to a stronger reaction to the allergen resulting in more prominent peri-bronchial and perivascular leukocytic infiltrates (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: Vitamin D deficiency led to a robust increase in total IgE levels in HDM-exposed mice.
source: Vitamin D deficiency led to a robust increase in total immunoglobulin (Ig)E levels (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA shown in Figure 3D

claim: Vitamin D deficiency resulted in higher total BAL leukocyte numbers in HDM-exposed mice.
source: Histological findings were associated with higher total BAL leukocyte (p = 0.0008) (Figure 3E), eosinophil (p = 0.0002) (Figure 3F), and lymphocyte (p = 0.0023) (Figure 3G) numbers in vitamin D-deficient mice, while neutrophil numbers were not affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by BAL cell counting shown in Figure 3E

claim: Vitamin D deficiency resulted in higher eosinophil numbers in BAL of HDM-exposed mice.
source: Histological findings were associated with higher total BAL leukocyte (p = 0.0008) (Figure 3E), eosinophil (p = 0.0002) (Figure 3F), and lymphocyte (p = 0.0023) (Figure 3G) numbers in vitamin D-deficient mice, while neutrophil numbers were not affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by BAL cell counting shown in Figure 3F

claim: Vitamin D deficiency resulted in higher lymphocyte numbers in BAL of HDM-exposed mice.
source: Histological findings were associated with higher total BAL leukocyte (p = 0.0008) (Figure 3E), eosinophil (p = 0.0002) (Figure 3F), and lymphocyte (p = 0.0023) (Figure 3G) numbers in vitamin D-deficient mice, while neutrophil numbers were not affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by BAL cell counting shown in Figure 3G

claim: Neutrophil numbers were not affected by vitamin D deficiency in HDM-exposed mice.
source: Histological findings were associated with higher total BAL leukocyte (p = 0.0008) (Figure 3E), eosinophil (p = 0.0002) (Figure 3F), and lymphocyte (p = 0.0023) (Figure 3G) numbers in vitamin D-deficient mice, while neutrophil numbers were not affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by BAL cell counting shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Th2 cell numbers were higher in HDM-exposed vitamin D-deficient mice.
source: Th2 cell numbers (p = 0.0127) were also higher in the HDM-exposed mice (Figure 3H) in a manner that was independent of T helper cell skewing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 3H

claim: The increased Th2 cell numbers in vitamin D-deficient HDM-exposed mice was independent of T helper cell skewing.
source: Th2 cell numbers (p = 0.0127) were also higher in the HDM-exposed mice (Figure 3H) in a manner that was independent of T helper cell skewing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C

claim: Differentiation and recruitment of Th17 and IL-10 producing CD4+ T cells was not affected by vitamin D deficiency.
source: Differentiation and recruitment of Th17 and IL-10 producing CD4+ T cells was not affected by vitamin D deficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: HDM sensitization and challenge of Vdr−/− mice led to an increased Th2 immune response.
source: As with the vitamin D-deficient mice, HDM sensitization and challenge of Vdr−/− mice led to an increased Th2 immune response.
evidence: Demonstrated by multiple measurements including IgE, BAL cells, and cytokine production

claim: The lung phenotype in Vdr−/− mice was marked by dense leukocytic infiltrates around and mucus plugs in the airways.
source: The lung phenotype in the Vdr−/− mice was marked by dense leukocytic infiltrates around and mucus plugs in the airways (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: Vdr−/− mice had increased total IgE titers after HDM exposure.
source: The augmented systemic and local immune response increased total IgE titers (p = 0.0489), and total BAL (p < 0.0001 vs WT HDM and p = 0.003 vs Vit D-deficient HDM), eosinophil (p < 0.0001 vs WT HDM and Vit D-deficient HDM), total lymphocytes (p = 0.0194 vs WT HDM and p = 0.0421 vs Vit D-deficient HDM), and Th2 cells (p = 0.0009 vs WT HDM) (Figure 3D–H).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA shown in Figure 3D

claim: Vdr−/− mice had increased total BAL cells after HDM exposure compared to WT and vitamin D-deficient mice.
source: The augmented systemic and local immune response increased total IgE titers (p = 0.0489), and total BAL (p < 0.0001 vs WT HDM and p = 0.003 vs Vit D-deficient HDM), eosinophil (p < 0.0001 vs WT HDM and Vit D-deficient HDM), total lymphocytes (p = 0.0194 vs WT HDM and p = 0.0421 vs Vit D-deficient HDM), and Th2 cells (p = 0.0009 vs WT HDM) (Figure 3D–H).
evidence: Demonstrated by BAL cell counting shown in Figure 3E

claim: Vdr−/− did not significantly affect recruitment of neutrophils, Treg, and Th17 cells.
source: Vdr−/− did not significantly affect recruitment of neutrophils, Treg, and Th17 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: Differential expression and enrichment analysis revealed dysregulation of several pathways implicated in Th2 cell activation, cytokine production, proliferation, and survival in vitamin D-deficient Th2 cells.
source: Differential expression and enrichment analysis revealed dysregulation of several pathways implicated in Th2 cell activation, cytokine production, proliferation, and survival with prominent changes in the IL-2/STAT5 pathway in vitamin D-deficient Th2 cells (p = 0.0014) (Figure 3J, Figure 3—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq and pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3J

claim: The IL-2/STAT5 pathway showed prominent changes in vitamin D-deficient Th2 cells.
source: Differential expression and enrichment analysis revealed dysregulation of several pathways implicated in Th2 cell activation, cytokine production, proliferation, and survival with prominent changes in the IL-2/STAT5 pathway in vitamin D-deficient Th2 cells (p = 0.0014) (Figure 3J, Figure 3—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq and pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3J

claim: Baseline expression of IL-2 was markedly increased at both the RNA and protein levels in vitamin D-deficient and Vdr−/− Th2 cells.
source: Baseline expression of IL-2 was markedly increased at both the RNA (p = 0.0286) and protein levels (p = 0.0079) in vitamin D-deficient and Vdr−/− Th2 cells (Figure 3K, L).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR and flow cytometry shown in Figure 3K, L

claim: Elevated IL-2 levels in vitamin D-deficient and Vdr−/− Th2 cells were accompanied by a sharp increase in IL-13 production.
source: In vitamin D-deficient and Vdr−/− Th2 cell in vitro incubation, the elevated IL-2 levels were accompanied by a sharp increase in IL-13 production (VitD deficient: p < 0.0001; Vdr−/−: p = 0.0141) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Calcitriol stimulation of Th2 cells affected several immune-related disease pathways, including asthma.
source: Calcitriol stimulation of Th2 cells affected several immune-related disease pathways, including asthma (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis highlighted the negative regulation of IL-2/Stat5 pathway in Th2 cells by calcitriol.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), performed on the differentially expressed genes, highlighted the negative regulation of IL-2/Stat5 pathway in Th2 cells by calcitriol (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by GSEA shown in Figure 4B

claim: Calcitriol stimulation suppressed the expression of Il2, Stat5a, and Stat5b genes in Th2 cells.
source: Calcitriol stimulation suppressed the expression of Il2 (p < 0.0001), Stat5a (p < 0.0008), and Stat5b (p < 0.0008) genes (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR shown in Figure 4C

claim: Calcitriol stimulation reduced levels of activated Itk (phospho-Itk) on a per cell basis.
source: Concordantly, levels of activated Itk (phospho-Itk) (p = 0.029) and expression of the IL2Rβ (CD25) (p = 0.0441) were reduced on a per cell basis (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 4D

claim: Calcitriol stimulation reduced expression of IL2Rβ (CD25) on a per cell basis.
source: Concordantly, levels of activated Itk (phospho-Itk) (p = 0.029) and expression of the IL2Rβ (CD25) (p = 0.0441) were reduced on a per cell basis (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 4D

claim: Activation of the vitamin D/Vdr pathway led to significant suppression of IL-13 production in CD4+ T cells.
source: Activation of the vitamin D/Vdr pathway led to significant suppression of IL-13 production in CD4+ T cells (p = 0.0012) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 4E

claim: Network analysis revealed the engagement of IL4R, IL2RA, CD28, and TNF receptors in control Th2 cells.
source: In control Th2 cells, our network analysis revealed the engagement of a variety of receptors including IL4R, IL2RA, CD28, and TNF receptors.
evidence: Demonstrated by computational network analysis of RNA-seq data

claim: The most active signaling paths in control Th2 cells highlighted the activation of STAT3, STAT5A/B, NFkB1, and IKZF1 transcription factors.
source: Downstream to these receptors, the most active signaling paths highlighted the activation of STAT3, STAT5A/B, NFkB1, and IKZF1 transcription factors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) via multiple adapter proteins of the TRAF and JAK family.
evidence: Demonstrated by computational network analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: After calcitriol stimulation, signal from IL4R, CD28, and TNFSF8 propagated over different interaction partners.
source: Conversely, after calcitriol stimulation, signal from IL4R, CD28, and TNFSF8 propagated over different interaction partners (Figure 4F).
evidence: Demonstrated by computational network analysis shown in Figure 4F

claim: Network analysis highlighted a central role of the transcriptional repressor IKZF1 (IKAROS) upon calcitriol stimulation.
source: Our network analysis highlighted a central role of the transcriptional repressor IKZF1 (IKAROS) upon calcitriol stimulation, which was targeted by multiple downstream mediators including IKZF3 (AIOLOS).
evidence: Demonstrated by computational network analysis

claim: AIOLOS is a direct interaction partner of IKAROS.
source: Notably, the IKZF3 gene encodes for the AIOLOS protein, a direct interaction partner of the IKZF1-encoded IKAROS.
evidence: Based on established protein-protein interaction knowledge

claim: IKAROS and AIOLOS, as homo- and heterodimers, suppress IL-2 expression on the transcriptional levels in mouse and human lymphocytes.
source: Both transcription factors, as homo- and heterodimers, suppress IL-2 expression on the transcriptional levels in mouse and human lymphocytes (Quintana et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quintana et al., 2012

claim: Calcitriol increased the number of edges connecting intermediate proteins to the transcriptional repressor IKAROS.
source: Calcitriol increased the number of edges connecting intermediate proteins to the transcriptional repressor IKAROS.
evidence: Demonstrated by computational network analysis

claim: Absence of STAT5A/B mediators in the active signaling paths of calcitriol-stimulated Th2 cells suggested repression of the Th2 cell STAT5 pathway with calcitriol.
source: Absence of STAT5A/B mediators in the active signaling paths of calcitriol-stimulated Th2 cells further suggested repression of the Th2 cell STAT5 pathway with calcitriol compared to control (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Inferred from computational network analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: Dietary supplementation with high vitamin D dose (4000 IU) decreased the inflammatory phenotype in HDM-exposed mice compared to the 400 and 1000 IU dosed animals.
source: In sharp contrast, dietary supplementation with the higher vitamin D dose (4000 IU) decreased the inflammatory phenotype in HDM-exposed mice compared to the 400 and 1000 IU dosed animals.
evidence: Demonstrated by histology and BAL cell analysis

claim: 4000 IU vitamin D supplementation decreased BAL leukocytes in HDM-exposed mice.
source: Concordant with the histological findings, BAL leukocytes (p < 0.0001) were decreased with marked reductions in BAL eosinophil (p = 0.0016), lymphocyte (p = 0.026), and neutrophil numbers (p = 0.0005) (Figure 5B, D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and the frequency of IL-13+ Th2 cells was significantly reduced in the lungs with 4000 IU of vitamin D (p = 0.0066 vs 400 IU HDM; p = 0.0011 vs 1000 IU HDM) (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by BAL cell counting shown in Figure 5B

claim: 4000 IU vitamin D supplementation resulted in marked reductions in BAL eosinophil, lymphocyte, and neutrophil numbers in HDM-exposed mice.
source: Concordant with the histological findings, BAL leukocytes (p < 0.0001) were decreased with marked reductions in BAL eosinophil (p = 0.0016), lymphocyte (p = 0.026), and neutrophil numbers (p = 0.0005) (Figure 5B, D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and the frequency of IL-13+ Th2 cells was significantly reduced in the lungs with 4000 IU of vitamin D (p = 0.0066 vs 400 IU HDM; p = 0.0011 vs 1000 IU HDM) (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by BAL cell counting shown in Figure 5B, D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: The frequency of IL-13+ Th2 cells was significantly reduced in the lungs with 4000 IU of vitamin D.
source: Concordant with the histological findings, BAL leukocytes (p < 0.0001) were decreased with marked reductions in BAL eosinophil (p = 0.0016), lymphocyte (p = 0.026), and neutrophil numbers (p = 0.0005) (Figure 5B, D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and the frequency of IL-13+ Th2 cells was significantly reduced in the lungs with 4000 IU of vitamin D (p = 0.0066 vs 400 IU HDM; p = 0.0011 vs 1000 IU HDM) (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 5E

claim: Dietary supplementation with high vitamin D levels increased Vdr expression in CD4+ T cells from HDM-exposed lungs.
source: Of note, dietary supplementation with high vitamin D levels, increased Vdr expression in CD4+ T cells from HDM-exposed lungs (p < 0.0001) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Gata3 expression on per cell basis was lower in 4000 IU Th2 cells.
source: Gata3 expression on per cell basis was lower in 4000 IU Th2 cells (p = 0.0286) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A

claim: 4000 IU Th2 cells had higher Vdr protein expression compared to 400 IU Th2 cells.
source: This was accompanied by higher Vdr protein expression (p = 0.0286) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: The expression of IL-2 and the Th2 cytokines IL-13 and IL-5 were lower in 4000 IU Th2 cultures.
source: The expression of IL-2 (p = 0.0004) and the Th2 cytokines IL-13 (p = 0.0159) and IL-5 (p = 0.0159) were lower in 4000 IU Th2 cultures (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–E

claim: Aiolos expression gradually increased under Th2-polarizing conditions in CD4+ T cells, starting as early as day 1 of in vitro culture.
source: Aiolos expression gradually increased under Th2-polarizing conditions in CD4+ T cells, starting as early as day 1 of in vitro culture (Figure 5F).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 5F

claim: Simultaneous exposure to calcitriol further increased Aiolos protein levels compared to vehicle in Th2 cells.
source: Simultaneous exposure to calcitriol further increased Aiolos protein levels compared to vehicle in Th2 cells (p = 0.0079) (Figure 5G).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 5G

claim: IL-2 production in control Ikzf3−/− Th2 cultures was significantly higher compared to WT Th2 cells.
source: IL-2 production in control Ikzf3−/− Th2 cultures was significantly higher compared to WT Th2 cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry

claim: Calcitriol significantly reduced IL-2 levels in both WT and Ikzf3−/− Th2 cells.
source: Calcitriol significantly reduced IL-2 levels in both, WT (p = 0.0001) and Ikzf3−/− Th2 cells (p = 0.0001) (Figure 5H); however, the suppressive effect of calcitriol on IL-2 production was significantly higher in WT Th2 cells (~65% inhibition) compared to Ikzf3−/− Th2 cells (~40% inhibition) (p = 0.0001) (Figure 5H).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 5H

claim: The suppressive effect of calcitriol on IL-2 production was significantly higher in WT Th2 cells (~65% inhibition) compared to Ikzf3−/− Th2 cells (~40% inhibition).
source: Calcitriol significantly reduced IL-2 levels in both, WT (p = 0.0001) and Ikzf3−/− Th2 cells (p = 0.0001) (Figure 5H); however, the suppressive effect of calcitriol on IL-2 production was significantly higher in WT Th2 cells (~65% inhibition) compared to Ikzf3−/− Th2 cells (~40% inhibition) (p = 0.0001) (Figure 5H).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry shown in Figure 5H

claim: Two enhancer sites in 17q12-21.1 were both predicted to interact with the ORMDL3 promoter region.
source: In particular, the two enhancer sites in 17q12-21.1 (GH17J039753 and GH17J039859) were both predicted to interact with the ORMDL3 promoter region (Figure 1B), and the enhancer site in 17q21.2 (GH17J042576) was predicted to interact with the STAT5A promoter region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on GeneHancer predictions shown in Figure 1B

claim: The enhancer site in 17q21.2 was predicted to interact with the STAT5A promoter region.
source: In particular, the two enhancer sites in 17q12-21.1 (GH17J039753 and GH17J039859) were both predicted to interact with the ORMDL3 promoter region (Figure 1B), and the enhancer site in 17q21.2 (GH17J042576) was predicted to interact with the STAT5A promoter region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on GeneHancer predictions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: VDR-binding sites coincide with CTCF- and IKZF3-binding sites, as well as H3K27ac peaks indicating active enhancer sites in both the 17q12-21.1 and 17q21.2 regions.
source: Importantly, in both the 17q12-21.1 and 17q21.2 regions, the VDR-binding sites coincide with CTCF- and IKZF3-binding sites, as well as H3K27ac peaks indicating active enhancer sites (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Vdr expression has been reported for airway epithelial cells and different immune cell types present in the lung.
source: Expression of Vdr has been reported for airway epithelial cells and different immune cell types present in the lung (Pfeffer and Hawrylowicz, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pfeffer and Hawrylowicz, 2018

claim: In lymphocytes, ex vivo and in vitro studies describe low baseline Vdr transcript expression levels that were transiently increased by activating signals and calcitriol stimulation.
source: In lymphocytes, ex vivo and in vitro studies describe low baseline Vdr transcript expression levels that were transiently increased by activating signals and calcitriol stimulation (Baeke et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baeke et al., 2010

claim: Differentiation of Th2 cells is driven by IL-4-induced Gata3 expression in naive CD4+ T cells.
source: Differentiation of Th2 cells is driven by IL-4-induced Gata3 expression in naive CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Based on established immunological knowledge

claim: Th2 cell differentiation depends on a positive feedforward loop by IL-2 and its downstream STAT5 signaling pathway for the effective expression of IL-4.
source: This process depends on a positive feedforward loop by IL-2 and its downstream STAT5 signaling pathway for the effective expression of IL-4 (Zhu et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2003

claim: AIOLOS has previously been shown to suppress IL-2 expression at the transcriptional level.
source: The transcription factor AIOLOS has previously been shown to suppress IL-2 expression at the transcriptional level (Quintana et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quintana et al., 2012
